question: Can a weight-tied decoder block learn a reusable algorithmic step from answer-only supervision at different depths, then extrapolate to longer inputs by running more loops?

key_findings.claim: The paper defines n-RASP-L tasks as computations expressible by repeatedly applying one finite RASP-L program a length-dependent number of times, optionally bracketed by fixed preprocessing and postprocessing.
key_findings.evidence: The authors construct iterative programs for copy, parity, and addition and use this class to connect variable-depth computation with a fixed-size decoder block. The definition is a representability condition; it does not prove gradient training will recover the stated program.

key_findings.claim: Step-dependent final-answer supervision gives the same block learning signals at multiple depths without revealing intermediate states.
key_findings.evidence: Training examples include input, target, and a known required step count T(n). The same decoder block is unrolled T times, with the loss applied only after the final loop. Because training lengths induce different T values, shared parameters receive terminal supervision after multiple depths; original-input injection and no positional encoding are additional architectural choices.

key_findings.claim: Looped full-output prediction substantially length-generalizes across six synthetic tasks, but the evidence does not isolate recurrence from the full-output format, input hints, curriculum, or oracle depth labels.
key_findings.evidence: On parity, copy, addition, multiplication, binary sum, and unique set, the adaptive looped model maintains near-perfect exact match well beyond the training-length boundary and outperforms NTP, pause-token, tied fixed-depth, and full-output variants in Figures 4 and 7. Addition is specially formatted with index hints; every method uses online generated data and a curriculum, and ablations show input injection helps.

key_findings.claim: The practical stopping rule is reliable mainly for tasks whose hidden state converges after reaching an answer.
key_findings.evidence: Oracle inference uses the known number of loops. The alternative chooses the step with maximum output confidence among a preset maximum. Batch-level selection over a same-length test set reaches near-perfect points in Figure 5, but per-instance selection degrades on non-convergent parity and binary-sum dynamics; batch-level selection is also transductive rather than an independent per-query halting mechanism.

key_findings.claim: Longer-input accuracy is purchased with superlinear recurrent attention cost and backpropagation depth.
key_findings.evidence: For test length n' and a(n') loops, oracle inference costs O(k a(n') n'^2); confidence search costs O(k N' n'^2). Fixed-depth NTP/FOP costs O(C n'^2), and the authors state their inference is slower because it uses more loops. Training backpropagates through all loops and is explicitly identified as computationally demanding.

key_findings.claim: Results are controlled algorithmic extrapolation, not evidence of open-domain LLM reasoning or universal length generalization.
key_findings.evidence: Models are 256-dimensional GPT-2-style blocks trained for 100k steps on unlimited synthetically sampled strings, with five runs and exact match over 6,400 samples. The task family assumes one repeated RASP-L loop and known training step counts; multi-loop programs, natural language, pretrained models, noisy supervision, and distribution shifts beyond length are not tested.

anchors.section: Appendix F training and evaluation details

method.core_idea: Train one decoder block at variable unroll depths so it learns a reusable computation that can be repeated more times on longer inputs.
method.mechanism: Use full-output prediction, weight-tied recurrence, original-input injection, NoPE, and a known example-specific terminal depth; at inference run the length-derived depth or search for maximum confidence.
assumptions: The target algorithm decomposes into repeated applications of one RASP-L step.
Training examples provide the correct number of loops even though intermediate states are absent.
Supervision across diverse lengths/depths induces a stable reusable step rather than depth-specific shortcuts.
The hidden dynamics remain useful when unrolled beyond depths seen in training.
Confidence is a valid unsupervised proxy for correct halting.

techniques.role: Allocates more sequential compute without increasing parameters.
Trains shared computation at different unroll depths using only final answers.
Lets every output position update in parallel after internal recurrent computation.
Prevents recurrent states from losing access to the problem instance.
Chooses an output from multiple inference depths without a target label.

evaluations.setting: Parity, copy, addition, multiplication, binary sum, and unique set trained on short synthetic inputs
evaluations.metric: Whole-sequence exact-match accuracy on longer lengths
evaluations.result: Adaptive looped FOP remains near-perfect far beyond the training boundary on most plotted ranges
evaluations.baseline: Vanilla NTP, NTP with pause tokens, tied-layer fixed NTP, FOP variants, and fixed-depth looped FOP

evaluations.result: Batch confidence nearly matches oracle; per-instance confidence works on convergent tasks but underperforms on parity and binary sum
Adaptive depth outperforms fixed depth, no input injection, pause-token compute, and fixed-step supervision

limitations: Author-stated: n-RASP-L cannot express sequential composition of multiple distinct loops.
Author-stated: backpropagating through many loops is expensive, and training lengths/depths were compute-limited.
Author-stated: ground-truth step counts are required during training.
Reviewer-identified: only small synthetic symbolic tasks with online unlimited data are evaluated.
Reviewer-identified: batch-level confidence halting uses an entire same-length test set and is not deployable for isolated heterogeneous requests.
Reviewer-identified: no mechanistic extraction verifies that the network learned the constructed n-RASP-L program rather than another extrapolating rule.
failure_modes: Non-convergent dynamics can become confidently wrong after the correct step and defeat per-instance halting.
Errors compound when the block is unrolled much farther than trained depths.
Tasks requiring branch-dependent or multiple-loop structure fall outside the model class.
Quadratic attention repeated O(n) times makes long-input compute roughly cubic for the studied algorithms.
Missing or inaccurate step-count labels train the final loss at the wrong hidden state.
Special input hints or NoPE assumptions may not transfer to natural tokenizations.
reusable_insights: Variable-depth terminal supervision can teach a recurrent transition without explicit traces when different examples terminate at different depths.
Length extrapolation should be reported jointly with sequential compute scaling and halting reliability.
Recurrent solvers need separate tests for answer convergence, overthinking, and per-instance stopping.
Representability by a concise program is useful task structure, but empirical recovery needs mechanistic verification.
open_questions: Can loop counts be learned from answer-only data without oracle depth annotations?
Can multiple learned transition operators be routed to express nested or sequential loops?
Does truncated or implicit differentiation preserve extrapolation while reducing memory?
Can a calibrated halting head outperform confidence search on non-convergent tasks?
Do pretrained language models gain real reasoning robustness from looped blocks under matched inference FLOPs?

competitive_landscape.title: Looped Transformers are Better at Learning Learning Algorithms
competitive_landscape.difference: Shows weight-tied loops learn iterative in-context learning algorithms with fewer parameters; the reviewed paper targets length extrapolation and adds variable-depth terminal supervision and halting.

competitive_landscape.title: What Algorithms can Transformers Learn? A Study in Length Generalization
competitive_landscape.difference: Links ordinary Transformer length generalization to short single-pass RASP-L programs and scratchpad design; the reviewed work extends the representable class by explicitly looping a RASP-L step.

competitive_landscape.title: Universal Length Generalization with Turing Programs
competitive_landscape.difference: Uses explicit Turing-machine-like intermediate text and covers arbitrary algorithms in principle; the reviewed work avoids intermediate supervision but assumes a single repeated operator and oracle training depths.

competitive_landscape.title: End-to-end Algorithm Synthesis with Recurrent Networks: Extrapolation without Overthinking
competitive_landscape.difference: Uses recall and progressive training to prevent degradation under extra recurrent steps; the reviewed method uses Transformer recurrence, input injection, variable terminal depths, and confidence halting.

competitive_landscape.title: NeuralSolver: Learning Algorithms For Consistent and Efficient Extrapolation Across General Tasks
competitive_landscape.difference: Supports same- and different-size input/output tasks through a multi-scale recurrent processing architecture; the reviewed work offers a sharper RASP-L characterization and decoder-only full-output formulation.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: Step-dependent supervision lets looped Transformers learn n-RASP-L algorithms without intermediate traces and achieve strong length generalization.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The formal n-RASP-L construction, variable-unroll loss, six-task curves, stopping analysis, and matched FOP ablations support the claim within controlled tasks.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The combination of RASP-L representability with variable-depth answer-only training is a clear contribution beyond prior looped Transformers. Scope is narrow: it assumes oracle depths and single-loop synthetic algorithms, so it does not yet establish general reasoning gains.

reviewer_notes: Read all 19 pages, including program listings, task curves, halting appendix, complexity, ablations, and training setup. Competitors were checked against primary OpenReview, arXiv, and NeurIPS records on 2026-08-23.
